title: Can, may, must, want
goal: Master the four small words that turn any verb into a request, a permission, an obligation or a wish — and learn to see the root hiding inside a long *me-* verb.
bekal: ask for permission and for help, correctly and politely
say what you can, must, may and want to do
strip *membeli*, *menulis*, *mengambil* back to the words you already know

notes: **Bisa is ability; boleh is permission.** *Bisa saya pakai?* asks whether the thing works or whether you are capable; *Boleh saya pakai?* asks whether you are allowed. In practice Indonesians blur them constantly — *Bisa pulang cepat?* here is really asking permission — but when you are the one asking a superior, *boleh* is the safer word.
**Boleh minta tolong? is the standard way to ask a favour.** Literally "may (I) ask for help?". Its answers are *boleh* / *silakan* (yes) or, softened, *maaf, sedang sibuk* (sorry, busy right now).

**Tolong + verb is the polite imperative.** *Tolong ambilkan* — "please fetch". A bare verb (*Ambil!*) is an order, and it lands hard. Adding *tolong* in front, or *ya* at the end, is the difference between asking and commanding.

**Ambilkan, not ambil.** That *-kan* on the end means "do it for someone". *Ambil* = take; *ambilkan* = fetch it for me. Same with *bukakan pintu* (open the door for me), *belikan* (buy it for me). It is the most useful suffix at your level after *-nya*.

**Sudah saya kirim** — notice the word order. Indonesian happily puts the object first and the doer straight before the verb, especially in the past. *Sudah saya kirim* ("already by-me sent") is completely natural and extremely common. It is the doorway into the passive system of Unit 19.

grammars.title: The four modal words
body: Each one sits directly in front of the verb, and the verb — as always — does not change.
after: ⚠️ **Tidak boleh is a prohibition, not a lack of ability.** *Saya tidak boleh makan itu* means "I'm not allowed to eat that" (a rule, a diet, a religion); *Saya tidak bisa makan itu* means "I can't" (allergy, impossible). Getting these two backwards can genuinely matter at a dinner table.
*Mau* and *ingin* both mean "want", but *mau* also means "about to" and is much more common in speech. *Ingin* is a little more formal and a little more wistful — closer to "wish".

grammars.title: Seeing the root inside a long verb
body: Indonesian dictionaries list roots, so being able to strip a prefix is the difference between finding a word and giving up. This is recognition, not production — you are not expected to build these yet.
after: The prefix is always *me-* underneath; what follows changes shape to fit the first sound of the root — *mem-* before b and p, *men-* before d and t, *meng-* before vowels, g and k, *meny-* before s. And in two of those cases the root's own first letter is swallowed: *tulis* → *menulis*, *sapu* → *menyapu*.

💬 **In everyday speech the prefix is often simply dropped.** *Saya beli* rather than *Saya membeli*; *Saya baca* rather than *Saya membaca*. This is not sloppy — it is how the language is actually spoken, and it means you can say almost everything at A1 with bare roots.

sections.title: Asking politely, in order of politeness

head: Indonesian
English
Register
rows: Could I ask you to fetch it?
Sorry, could you help a moment?

blocks.text: Notice that Indonesian gets politeness from **added words**, not from changed verb forms. There is no conditional, no subjunctive, nothing to conjugate. You stack *maaf*, *boleh*, *minta tolong* and *ya* until the sentence is soft enough for the situation.
And the replies you will hear: *Boleh* (sure), *Silakan* (go ahead), *Tentu* (certainly), *Sebentar, ya* (one moment), *Maaf, tidak bisa* (sorry, I can't).
Public notices are where *boleh*, *harus* and *dilarang* live. You will not write these, but you must read them.

*WC* is pronounced **wé-sé**, from the Dutch, and everybody understands it. *Kamar kecil* — "small room" — is the polite euphemism. Asking *Permisi, WC di mana?* will never be misunderstood anywhere in the country.

items: Saya tidak ____ berenang. Saya takut air.
Maaf, saya tidak ____ datang. Saya sakit.
